title: A Podcast on Zoot Suits? Yes
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a shout-out to listener Martin van Nostrin's band and a roundup of dumb laws, then focus on why zoot suits were banned in Los Angeles. They describe the zoot suit's look and origins (Harlem nightclub scene, Cab Calloway, disputed Gainesville, Georgia story), its shift to a symbol of defiance among Mexican American pachucos in Los Angeles, the wartime fabric rationing and the War Production Board's streamlined suit, the Sleepy Lagoon case, the June 1943 clashes between sailors and Latino youths culminating in the Zoot Suit Riots, and the city ordinance banning zoot suits. They close with a note on later legacies, listener mail about 1940s slang and a polygraph experience, and sign-off information.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and dumb laws
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck greet listeners and thank Martin van Nostrin for a band CD and T-shirts. Chuck reads a list of dumb laws from US states and cities, including the Los Angeles zoot suit ban, which sets up the episode.

segments.title: What a zoot suit looks like
segments.summary: The hosts describe zoot suits from the 1930s: broad padded shoulders, long-waisted coats, high-waisted pants that balloon and taper at the ankle, and pocket chains and hats. Cab Calloway's slang description and the original name 'drape suits' are mentioned.

segments.title: Origins: Harlem and the Gainesville story
segments.summary: The zoot suit grew out of the Harlem Renaissance club scene and was associated with figures like Cab Calloway and Malcolm X. The New York Times repeated a story that bus worker Clyde Duncan bought one in Gainesville, Georgia, but historians found the origin murky.

segments.title: World War II rationing and zoot suit defiance
segments.summary: In Los Angeles the style was taken up by Mexican American pachucos and became political. Because zoot suits used lots of cloth during WWII rationing, they were seen as unpatriotic, and the War Production Board promoted a streamlined suit. Zoot suits became a symbol of defiance, and bootleg tailors made them illegally.

segments.title: Pachucos, racism and the Sleepy Lagoon case
segments.summary: Second-generation Latino American youths, many of them latchkey kids, were called pachucos and linked by newspapers to crime. Racial tension grew in Los Angeles. The Sleepy Lagoon case, in which Jose Diaz was found dead at a reservoir after a party, led to nine young Mexican Americans being wrongly convicted before an appeal overturned it.

segments.title: The Zoot Suit Riots of 1943
segments.summary: Servicemen in Los Angeles clashed with Latino youths in zoot suits in late May and early June. Off-duty and on-duty police calling themselves the Vengeance Squad beat Latinos, then about two hundred sailors attacked Mexican kids and others, stripping and burning clothes. Police did not arrest the servicemen. The city council banned zoot suits, and about 150 people were injured with over 500 Latinos arrested.

segments.title: Legacy of zoot suits and related films
segments.summary: The hosts note that zoot suits later symbolized defiance among Soviet teenagers and that the juvenile delinquency theme inspired films such as Rebel Without a Cause, The Wild Ones, and I Was a Teenage Werewolf.

segments.title: Search tips and show sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts suggest searches for more on zoot suits and Cab Calloway's slang dictionary, then mention upcoming topics like the Stonewall riots.

segments.title: Listener mail: slang, polygraphs, and sign-off
segments.summary: Listeners share 1940s slang such as moo juice and crumb crushers, and a polygraph examinee describes his experience, including the pad that registered fidgeting. Matthew asks for tribal drums. The hosts give contact details and promote their video podcast.
